title: ‘Stereotype’ and ‘cliché’ began as printers’ words for cast metal plates

cover.alt: Black-and-white film still: a heavy metal casting machine with a tall curved casting box, a worker standing beside it, in a 1937 newspaper print shop.

body: For much of the 19th and 20th centuries, big newspapers didn’t print straight from their type. They pressed a mould of each page, the **flong**, out of layers of papier-mâché, then cast that mould in **type metal**, an alloy of lead, tin and antimony. The result was a solid plate, a **stereotype**, which could be curved to fit the cylinders of a fast rotary press. One flong could make many identical plates for several presses at once, and the costly type was freed for the next edition. Because a stereotype repeats the same image over and over, the word became a metaphor for ideas repeated without change, and **cliché**, the printers’ other word for it, took a similar path.

slides.label: plates cast for a single Sunday edition of The New York Times
slides.text: In the 1940s it used about 45 tons of type metal a night, 150 on Saturdays. Once a page was set, the team had 15 minutes to mould, cast, trim and cool its plates and mount them.

slides.question: Where does the word ‘cliché’ come from?
options: The sound of casting a plate
slides.explanation: It imitated the sound of striking a block into molten type metal. ‘Stereotype’ comes from Greek words meaning ‘solid’ and ‘impression’.

slides.heading: Why the plates disappeared
slides.text: Offset printing and phototypesetting made cast plates unnecessary, and computer typesetting took over in the 1970s. The printers’ words outlived the process: today a stereotype or a cliché is an idea or phrase used so often that it no longer says anything new.
